title: Not a Fan Club
subtitle: 1 Corinthians 1:1–17
description: A thanksgiving full of grace, then the first report: the church that Paul planted is sorting itself into camps behind its teachers.
paragraphs: The letter to Corinth opens with two names. Paul had planted this church himself, in the long stay Acts records, and he now wrote from Ephesus, where the end of the letter says he was staying until Pentecost. The first name is his own, stated the way he always stated it: “Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and our brother Sosthenes,” and the second name would have stopped a Corinthian reader. Acts had used it in this same city, for the synagogue ruler seized and beaten in front of Gallio's judgment seat. The letter gives its co-sender that name and calls him brother, and says nothing more about him.

The address reaches past one congregation: “To the church of God in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus and called to be holy,” and then wider still, “together with all those everywhere who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, their Lord and ours:”. Then the greeting every letter of his carries: “Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

What follows is thanksgiving, and it is generous. “I always thank my God for you because of the grace He has given you in Christ Jesus.” Paul tells them what that grace had done in them: “For in Him you have been enriched in every way, in all speech and all knowledge,” because, he says, “our testimony about Christ was confirmed in you.” Nothing was missing: “Therefore you do not lack any spiritual gift”. The promise under it all is God's own keeping: “He will sustain you to the end, so that you will be blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.” And the ground of the promise: “God, who has called you into fellowship with His Son Jesus Christ our Lord, is faithful.”

Then the letter turns, on one report. “I appeal to you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree together, so that there may be no divisions among you and that you may be united in mind and conviction.” The appeal names its source the way the letter always names its sources: “My brothers, some from Chloe’s household have informed me that there are quarrels among you.” What the household reported, the letter does not dramatize. It answers it.

The quarrels had slogans. “What I mean is this: Individuals among you are saying, ‘I follow Paul,’ ‘I follow Apollos,’ ‘I follow Cephas,’ or ‘I follow Christ.’” The church Paul planted was sorting itself into camps behind the men who had taught it, and the last slogan shows how far it had gone: even Christ's name had been made into one faction's banner among the others.

Paul answers with three questions, and they do the whole argument at once: “Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Were you baptized into the name of Paul?” A divided Christ, a crucified Paul, a baptism into a teacher's name: put that way, the slogans collapse under their own weight. The cross belongs to one name, and baptism does too.

Then, almost as a relief, he counts his own baptisms and finds the list short. “I thank God that I did not baptize any of you except Crispus and Gaius,” he writes, “so no one can say that you were baptized into my name.” One more household comes back to him as he writes: “Yes, I also baptized the household of Stephanas;” and then the honest limit of his memory: “beyond that I do not remember if I baptized anyone else.” No one in Corinth could build a Paul party on a Paul baptism, because there were barely any to build on.

The last verse of the opening draws the line the whole letter will walk. Baptizing was never the errand: “For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel, not with words of wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.” Not with words of wisdom: in a city sorting itself by its favorite speakers, Paul refuses to compete as one. The message he is about to set against every slogan is not his wisdom. It is the cross, and the letter turns to it next.

title: The Foolishness of the Cross
subtitle: 1 Corinthians 1:18–31
description: One event, two verdicts: to the world a crucified Messiah is foolishness, and God chose the foolish and the weak on purpose.
paragraphs: The letter's opening ended on a refusal: Paul would not preach with words of wisdom. Now he says why, and the reason is the message itself. “For the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.” One event, two verdicts. To the world sorting itself by wisdom, a crucified Messiah is nonsense. To those being saved, the same cross is God's power at work.

Paul does not argue the point from himself. He points to what stands written: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise; the intelligence of the intelligent I will frustrate.” Then the questions come in a row, addressed to a world proud of its learning: “Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the philosopher of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?”

The failure, Paul says, was built into the arrangement: “For since in the wisdom of God the world through its wisdom did not know Him, God was pleased through the foolishness of what was preached to save those who believe.” Wisdom had its chance to reach God and never arrived. So God saved people by the route no one would have chosen: a preached message the world calls foolish.

He names the two hungers the message refuses to feed. “Jews demand signs and Greeks search for wisdom,” and against both stands one sentence: “but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles,”. The preaching does not adjust itself to the audience's test. And yet it lands, on the people neither test predicted: “but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.” What the cross actually is turns out to be greater than what either side was asking for: “For the foolishness of God is wiser than man’s wisdom, and the weakness of God is stronger than man’s strength.”

Then Paul turns the argument on the Corinthians themselves, and it becomes personal. “Brothers, consider the time of your calling: Not many of you were wise by human standards; not many were powerful; not many were of noble birth.” The church quarreling over its teachers was not made of the impressive. That was not an accident of Corinth. It was the method: “But God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise; God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong.” And further down still: “He chose the lowly and despised things of the world, and the things that are not, to nullify the things that are,”. The purpose of the choosing is stated plainly: “so that no one may boast in His presence.”

Everything the Corinthians have, they have from that choosing: “It is because of Him that you are in Christ Jesus, who has become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and redemption.” Wisdom from God, not achieved by men: that is where boasting goes to die. The chapter closes by handing the slogan-writers a slogan of their own to carry, the one that stands written: “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord.”

title: The Mind of Christ
subtitle: 1 Corinthians 2:1–16
description: Paul's trembling preaching, the hidden wisdom the rulers never saw, and the Spirit who knows the thoughts of God.
paragraphs: Paul now defends his own preaching by describing it, and the description is a confession of weakness. “When I came to you, brothers, I did not come with eloquence or wisdom as I proclaimed to you the testimony about God.” There had been a decision before he ever reached Corinth: “For I resolved to know nothing while I was with you except Jesus Christ and Him crucified.” And the manner matched the message: “I came to you in weakness and fear, and with much trembling.”

The lack of polish was not a failure of skill. It was the strategy: “My message and my preaching were not with persuasive words of wisdom, but with a demonstration of the Spirit’s power,”. The reason stands right behind it: “so that your faith would not rest on men’s wisdom, but on God’s power.” Faith built on a speaker's brilliance stands or falls with the speaker. Paul wanted theirs standing on something else.

But the letter does speak of wisdom, and Paul will not let the word go. “Among the mature, however, we speak a message of wisdom”, “but not the wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are coming to nothing.” The wisdom is older than the age that rejects it: “No, we speak of the mysterious and hidden wisdom of God, which He destined for our glory before time began.” Hidden, and hidden with consequences the rulers never saw: “None of the rulers of this age understood it. For if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.”

What no one saw, Scripture had already said: “No eye has seen, no ear has heard, no heart has imagined, what God has prepared for those who love Him.” Then the turn that carries the whole chapter: “But God has revealed it to us by the Spirit. The Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God.”

Paul argues it from ordinary life. A man's thoughts are his own, known from inside: “For who among men knows the thoughts of man except his own spirit within him? So too, no one knows the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God.” And the gift given to believers is exactly that Spirit: “We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we may understand what God has freely given us.” The teaching follows the gift: “And this is what we speak, not in words taught us by human wisdom, but in words taught by the Spirit, expressing spiritual truths in spiritual words.”

That is why the same words divide their hearers. “The natural man does not accept the things that come from the Spirit of God. For they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually discerned.” Set against him: “The spiritual man judges all things, but he himself is not subject to anyone’s judgment.”

The chapter ends with a written question and a staggering answer. The question stands in Scripture's own words: “For who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct Him?” No one instructs God. And then Paul, without pausing, says of the people he is writing to: “But we have the mind of Christ.” The letter will spend its next breath showing how far the Corinthians still are from living like it.

title: Milk, Fields, and Fire
subtitle: 1 Corinthians 3:1–23
description: Infants on milk, servants in a field, builders on one foundation, and a temple the factions are damaging.
paragraphs: For all the talk of the Spirit, Paul cannot address the Corinthians as spiritual people. “Brothers, I could not address you as spiritual, but as worldly”, “as infants in Christ.” The diet gives them away: “I gave you milk, not solid food, for you were not yet ready for solid food. In fact, you are still not ready,”. And the proof is not what they fail to understand. It is how they treat each other: “for you are still worldly. For since there is jealousy and dissension among you, are you not worldly? Are you not walking in the way of man?” The slogans themselves are the evidence: “For when one of you says, ‘I follow Paul,’ and another, ‘I follow Apollos,’ are you not mere men?”

So Paul shrinks the teachers to their actual size, starting with himself. “What then is Apollos? And what is Paul? They are servants through whom you believed, as the Lord has assigned to each his role.” Then the first picture, a field: “I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow.” The workers differ; the growth belongs to neither: “So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God, who makes things grow.” They are not rivals but one crew: “He who plants and he who waters are one in purpose, and each will be rewarded according to his own labor.” And the summary line holds both the honor and the limit: “For we are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field, God’s building.”

The second picture is the building, and it comes with a warning to everyone who builds. Paul's own part is named: “By the grace God has given me, I laid a foundation as an expert builder, and someone else is building on it. But each one must be careful how he builds.” The foundation allows no substitutes: “For no one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ.”

What men build on it varies, and the variation will be tested: “If anyone builds on this foundation using gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or straw,” then a day of inspection is coming: “his workmanship will be evident, because the Day will bring it to light. It will be revealed with fire, and the fire will prove the quality of each man’s work.” Two outcomes stand side by side: “If what he has built survives, he will receive a reward.” And: “If it is burned up, he will suffer loss. He himself will be saved, but only as if through the flames.”

Then the building turns out to be the readers themselves, and the warning sharpens: “Do you not know that you yourselves are God’s temple, and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” “If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him; for God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple.” The factions quarreling in Corinth were not rearranging furniture. They were damaging the house God lives in.

The chapter closes where the letter's first argument began, with wisdom, and with Scripture quoted twice against self-deception: “Let no one deceive himself. If any of you thinks he is wise in this age, he should become a fool, so that he may become wise.” “For the wisdom of this world is foolishness in God’s sight.” As it is written: “He catches the wise in their craftiness.” And again: “The Lord knows that the thoughts of the wise are futile.”

So the boasting in men ends, because the arithmetic runs the other way: “Therefore, stop boasting in men. All things are yours,”, “whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future. All of them belong to you,”. The teachers were never the prize. They were part of the inheritance: “and you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God.”

title: Stewards and Spectacles
subtitle: 1 Corinthians 4:1–21
description: Judgment deferred to the Lord, the apostles displayed as the world's refuse, and a father's choice: a rod, or love.
paragraphs: The teachers are servants, and now Paul gives their job its proper title. “So then, men ought to regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God.” A steward manages another man's house, and the one requirement is stated flatly: “Now it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.” Found faithful by the house's owner, not by the household's applause.

So Paul dismisses every court the Corinthians might convene, including his own: “I care very little, however, if I am judged by you or by any human court. In fact, I do not even judge myself.” Even a clear conscience settles nothing: “My conscience is clear, but that does not vindicate me. It is the Lord who judges me.” The verdict waits for the only judge with full evidence: “Therefore judge nothing before the appointed time; wait until the Lord comes. He will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and will expose the motives of men’s hearts. At that time each will receive his praise from God.”

The whole picture, he tells them, was drawn for their benefit: “Brothers, I have applied these things to myself and Apollos for your benefit, so that you may learn from us not to go beyond what is written. Then you will not take pride in one man over another.” Then the questions that strip the boasting down: “For who makes you so superior? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not?”

Then the irony comes out, and it is some of the sharpest writing in the letter. “Already you have all you want. Already you have become rich. Without us, you have become kings. How I wish you really were kings, so that we might be kings with you!” Against their throne stands the apostles' procession: “For it seems to me that God has displayed us apostles at the end of the procession, like prisoners appointed for death. We have become a spectacle to the whole world, to angels as well as to men.” The contrasts run in pairs: “We are fools for Christ, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are honored, but we are dishonored.” And the apostolic life itself, undressed: “To this very hour we are hungry and thirsty, we are poorly clothed, we are brutally treated, we are homeless.” “We work hard with our own hands. When we are vilified, we bless; when we are persecuted, we endure it;” “when we are slandered, we answer gently. Up to this moment we have become the scum of the earth, the refuse of the world.”

The tone then changes completely, because the relationship is not what the irony suggests: “I am not writing this to shame you, but to warn you as my beloved children.” Guardians can be hired by the thousand: “Even if you have ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel.” So the request a father can make: “Therefore I urge you to imitate me.”

Timothy is already on the road as the letter's living reminder: “That is why I have sent you Timothy, my beloved and faithful child in the Lord. He will remind you of my way of life in Christ Jesus, which is exactly what I teach everywhere in every church.” But some in Corinth were counting on Paul never coming at all: “Some of you have become arrogant, as if I were not coming to you.” He is coming: “But I will come to you shortly, if the Lord is willing, and then I will find out not only what these arrogant people are saying, but what power they have.” For the measure is not talk: “For the kingdom of God is not a matter of talk but of power.” The chapter ends by handing them the choice of his arrival: “Which do you prefer? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and with a gentle spirit?”

title: Purge the Leaven
subtitle: 1 Corinthians 5:1–13
description: A case the church is proud of instead of grieved by, a little leaven through the whole batch, and an earlier letter corrected.
paragraphs: The letter now takes up a report worse than the quarrels, and Paul states it in the flat words it deserves: “It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is intolerable even among pagans: A man has his father’s wife.” The letter never names the man, and it never gives the woman a word. What shocks Paul is not only the act. It is the church's response to it: “And you are proud! Shouldn’t you rather have been stricken with grief and have removed from your fellowship the man who did this?”

Paul renders his verdict from Ephesus as if he were standing in the room: “Although I am absent from you in body, I am present with you in spirit, and I have already pronounced judgment on the one who did this, just as if I were present.” The sentence is to be carried out assembled, in the Lord's name and power: “When you are assembled in the name of our Lord Jesus and I am with you in spirit, along with the power of the Lord Jesus,”, “hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved on the Day of the Lord.” The letter states the aim inside the sentence itself: destruction of the flesh, aimed at a spirit saved on the Day. How it worked out, this letter does not say. Paul does not say it here, and no later letter's word is imported into this one.

Then the picture that explains why one tolerated case is never only one: “Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough?” The command follows the picture: “Get rid of the old leaven, that you may be a new unleavened batch, as you really are. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.” The feast they are to keep is a life: “Therefore let us keep the feast, not with the old bread, leavened with malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth.”

The command reaches back, and here the letter shows one of its seams. Paul had written before: “I wrote you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people.” That earlier letter is not in Scripture, and this one never reconstructs it. It only corrects how it was read: “I was not including the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters. In that case you would have to leave this world.” The line runs through the church's own fellowship, not around the world: “But now I am writing you not to associate with anyone who claims to be a brother but is sexually immoral or greedy, an idolater or a verbal abuser, a drunkard or a swindler. With such a man do not even eat.”

The boundary of judgment is drawn as plainly as the command: “What business of mine is it to judge those outside the church? Are you not to judge those inside?” “God will judge those outside.” And the chapter closes with the old command from Deuteronomy standing as the letter's last word on the case: “Expel the wicked man from among you.”

title: Such Were Some of You
subtitle: 1 Corinthians 6:1–20
description: Brother suing brother before unbelievers, a catalog answered by a past tense, and the body as a temple with a price paid.
paragraphs: From the case inside the church, the letter turns to a scandal outside it: believers hauling each other into pagan courts. “If any of you has a grievance against another, how dare he go to law before the unrighteous instead of before the saints!” Paul argues from the church's future to its present: “Do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if you are to judge the world, are you not competent to judge trivial cases?” And higher still: “Do you not know that we will judge angels? How much more the things of this life!”

The practice on the ground shames the claim: “So if you need to settle everyday matters, do you appoint as judges those of no standing in the church?” “I say this to your shame. Is there really no one among you wise enough to arbitrate between his brothers?” “Instead, one brother goes to law against another, and this in front of unbelievers!” The lawsuit itself is already the loss, whoever wins it: “The very fact that you have lawsuits among you means that you are thoroughly defeated already. Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be cheated?” And the church's own conduct is worse than its courts: “Instead, you yourselves cheat and do wrong, even against your own brothers!”

Then the warning, quoted whole the way the letter gives it, because the next sentence is its answer: “Do you not know that the wicked will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: Neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who submit to or perform homosexual acts,”, “nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor verbal abusers, nor swindlers, will inherit the kingdom of God.” And then the sentence the whole catalog exists for: “And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.” Were. The list is a past tense the Corinthians used to live in.

The chapter's second half takes up another Corinthian slogan, and the letter quotes it in the Corinthians' own quotation marks: “‘Everything is permissible for me,’ but not everything is beneficial. ‘Everything is permissible for me,’ but I will not be mastered by anything.” And its companion: “‘Food for the stomach and the stomach for food,’ but God will destroy them both.” Against the slogans Paul sets the body's purpose: “The body is not intended for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.” And its future: “By His power God raised the Lord from the dead, and He will raise us also.”

What the body is now makes the Corinthian practice unthinkable: “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and unite them with a prostitute? Never!” The union is real, whichever way it runs: “Or don’t you know that he who unites himself with a prostitute is one with her in body? For it is said, ‘The two will become one flesh.’” “But he who unites himself with the Lord is one with Him in spirit.”

So the command is not a debate. It is flight: “Flee from sexual immorality. Every other sin a man can commit is outside his body, but he who sins sexually sins against his own body.” And the reason returns to the temple of chapter 3, now located in each believer: “Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have received from God? You are not your own;” “you were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God with your body.”

title: Called as You Are
subtitle: 1 Corinthians 7:1–40
description: The Corinthians' own questions: marriage, singleness, mixed homes, slavery and freedom, and the shortness of the time.
paragraphs: Here the letter changes key, and Paul marks the change himself: “Now for the matters you wrote about:”. The Corinthians had sent questions, and the first of them concerned marriage itself. Someone in Corinth had put it as a slogan: “It is good to abstain from sexual relations.” Paul's answer neither blesses the slogan nor buries it. Because of the immorality loose in the city, “each man should have his own wife, and each woman her own husband.” Marriage is a mutual giving, stated with a symmetry the ancient world rarely heard: “The husband should fulfill his marital duty to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband.” “The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife.” Even abstinence inside marriage is bounded: “Do not deprive each other, except by mutual consent and for a time, so you may devote yourselves to prayer. Then come together again, so that Satan will not tempt you through your lack of self-control.” And Paul labels his own words as he goes: “I say this as a concession, not as a command.”

His own state is singleness, and he does not hide his preference: “I wish that all men were as I am. But each man has his own gift from God; one has this gift, another has that.” To the unmarried and widows the counsel matches his own life: “It is good for them to remain unmarried, as I am.” With the honest alternative beside it: “But if they cannot control themselves, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn with passion.”

For the married, the source of the word changes, and Paul says so in the sentence: “To the married I give this command (not I, but the Lord): A wife must not separate from her husband.” The command has a door in it: “But if she does, she must remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband. And a husband must not divorce his wife.” Then the cases Jesus never addressed, and the label changes again: “To the rest I say this (I, not the Lord): If a brother has an unbelieving wife and she is willing to live with him, he must not divorce her.” The mixed marriage is not contamination: “For the unbelieving husband is sanctified through his believing wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified through her believing husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy.” But if the unbelieving partner walks away, the believer is not chained to the door: “But if the unbeliever leaves, let him go. The believing brother or sister is not bound in such cases. God has called you to live in peace.” The chapter leaves the question open in both directions: “How do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?”

Then the principle that governs the whole chapter, stated as a rule for every church: “Regardless, each one should lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him and to which God has called him. This is what I prescribe in all the churches.” Circumcision changes nothing either way: “Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing. Keeping God’s commandments is what counts.” Slavery changes nothing either: “Each one should remain in the situation he was in when he was called.” “Were you a slave when you were called? Do not let it concern you”, “but if you can gain your freedom, take the opportunity.” The standings invert in Christ: “For he who was a slave when he was called by the Lord is the Lord’s freedman. Conversely, he who was a free man when he was called is Christ’s slave.” “You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of men.”

The last question concerns the unmarried, and here Paul is careful about his authority: “Now about virgins, I have no command from the Lord, but I give a judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy.” His judgment leans on the hour: “Because of the present crisis, I think it is good for a man to remain as he is.” Marriage is no sin, and he says so twice. But it carries trouble he wants to spare them, because the horizon is short: “What I am saying, brothers, is that the time is short. From now on those who have wives should live as if they had none;” “those who weep, as if they did not; those who are joyful, as if they were not; those who make a purchase, as if they had nothing;” “and those who use the things of this world, as if not dependent on them. For this world in its present form is passing away.”

The stated aim is freedom, not restriction: “I want you to be free from concern.” The unmarried man's concerns run one way, the married man's are divided between the Lord's work and his wife, and the same is said of women, in the same even terms. “I am saying this for your own good, not to restrict you, but in order to promote proper decorum and undivided devotion to the Lord.” The betrothed may marry without sin; the man who holds his resolve does well, and not marrying does even better. A widow is free to remarry, “as long as he belongs to the Lord,” and Paul closes with his judgment and his confidence together: “In my judgment, however, she is happier if she remains as she is. And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.”

title: Knowledge Puffs Up, Love Builds Up
subtitle: 1 Corinthians 8:1–13
description: An idol is nothing, and a brother is not: knowledge that destroys the weak is answered by a man giving up meat forever.
paragraphs: The next written question gets its own seam: “Now about food sacrificed to idols:”. Meat from the temples filled Corinth's markets, and the church's knowledgeable members had a slogan ready: “We know that we all have knowledge.” Paul quotes it back with the verdict attached: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” And the limit on all knowing: “The one who thinks he knows something does not yet know as he ought to know.” Against it, a different kind of being known: “But the one who loves God is known by God.”

On the facts, Paul concedes the knowledge completely: “So about eating food sacrificed to idols: We know that an idol is nothing at all in the world, and that there is no God but one.” The so-called gods get their exact weight: “For even if there are so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth (as there are many so-called gods and lords),” “yet for us there is but one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we exist. And there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came and through whom we exist.”

Then the turn the whole chapter exists for: “But not everyone has this knowledge. Some people are still so accustomed to idols that they eat such food as if it were sacrificed to an idol. And since their conscience is weak, it is defiled.” The food itself is neutral ground: “But food does not bring us closer to God: We are no worse if we do not eat, and no better if we do.” The danger is not in the eating. It is in the watching: “Be careful, however, that your freedom does not become a stumbling block to the weak.”

Paul draws the scene. A brother whose conscience is still bound to the idol sees a knowledgeable Christian at table in the temple itself: “For if someone with a weak conscience sees you who are well informed eating in an idol’s temple, will he not be encouraged to eat food sacrificed to idols?” The knowledge that was supposed to free becomes the instrument of a fall: “So this weak brother, for whom Christ died, is destroyed by your knowledge.” And the sin registers higher than the brother: “By sinning against your brothers in this way and wounding their weak conscience, you sin against Christ.”

The chapter ends with Paul applying the rule to himself first, in the most absolute form in the letter: “Therefore, if what I eat causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat again, so that I will not cause him to stumble.” Never again, rather than one brother. The next chapter shows the same man surrendering far more than meat.

title: Woe to Me If I Do Not Preach
subtitle: 1 Corinthians 9:1–27
description: Every right of an apostle established from Scripture, and every one of them surrendered; the athlete who can be disqualified.
paragraphs: Paul has just surrendered his dinner for a brother's conscience. Now he defends a much larger surrender, and he opens with his credentials stated as questions: “Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are you yourselves not my workmanship in the Lord?” Whatever others decide, Corinth is settled evidence: “Even if I am not an apostle to others, surely I am to you. For you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.”

The defense is a list of rights, each one real. “This is my defense to those who scrutinize me:” “Have we no right to food and to drink?” “Have we no right to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the Lord’s brothers and Cephas?” “Or are Barnabas and I the only apostles who must work for a living?” Ordinary life backs every claim: “Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who tends a flock and does not drink of its milk?” And Scripture backs them too. “Do I say this from a human perspective? Doesn’t the Law say the same thing?” In the Law of Moses it stands written: “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.” The ox was never the point: “Isn’t He actually speaking on our behalf? Indeed, this was written for us, because when the plowman plows and the thresher threshes, they should also expect to share in the harvest.” The temple runs on the same rule: “Do you not know that those who work in the temple eat of its food, and those who serve at the altar partake of its offerings?” And the Lord himself set the pattern: “In the same way, the Lord has prescribed that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel.”

Every right established, Paul gives them all away: “But I have not used any of these rights. And I am not writing this to suggest that something be done for me. Indeed, I would rather die than let anyone nullify my boast.” The preaching is not a career he chose; it owns him: “Yet when I preach the gospel, I have no reason to boast, because I am obligated to preach. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!” His pay is the refusal of pay: “What then is my reward? That in preaching the gospel I may offer it free of charge, and so not use up my rights in preaching it.”

The freedom he will not use for money, he spends entirely on people: “Though I am free of obligation to anyone, I make myself a slave to everyone, to win as many as possible.” Then the great catalogue of his shapeshifting, each form adopted for the people inside it: “To the Jews I became like a Jew, to win the Jews. To those under the law I became like one under the law (though I myself am not under the law), to win those under the law.” “To those without the law I became like one without the law (though I am not outside the law of God but am under the law of Christ), to win those without the law.” “To the weak I became weak, to win the weak. I have become all things to all people so that by all possible means I might save some.” The motive is named once, for all of it: “I do all this for the sake of the gospel, so that I may share in its blessings.”

Corinth knew the games; their own Isthmian contests were famous across Greece. Paul closes with the athlete he himself is. “Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? Run in such a way as to take the prize.” The athletes' discipline is total, and their crown rots: “Everyone who competes in the games trains with strict discipline. They do it for a crown that is perishable, but we do it for a crown that is imperishable.” So the apostle trains like a man who can lose: “Therefore I do not run aimlessly; I do not fight like I am beating the air.” “No, I discipline my body and make it my slave, so that after I have preached to others, I myself will not be disqualified.” The next words of the letter turn that warning on Israel itself, whose story Paul knew better than anyone.

title: The Rock Was Christ
subtitle: 1 Corinthians 10:1–11:1
description: Israel's privileges and Israel's graveyard, two tables no one can sit at together, and freedom governed by another's conscience.
paragraphs: The man who feared being disqualified now opens Israel's history and reads it as a warning addressed to himself and to Corinth alike. “I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our forefathers were all under the cloud, and that they all passed through the sea.” The privileges were universal: “They were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea.” “They all ate the same spiritual food” “and drank the same spiritual drink; for they drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ.” And the outcome was a graveyard: “Nevertheless, God was not pleased with most of them, for they were struck down in the wilderness.”

Paul states what the history is for: “These things took place as examples to keep us from craving evil things as they did.” Then the examples march, each with its toll. Idolatry, with Scripture's own scene quoted: “Do not be idolaters, as some of them were. As it is written:” “The people sat down to eat and drink and got up to indulge in revelry.” Sexual immorality: “We should not commit sexual immorality, as some of them did, and in one day twenty-three thousand of them died.” Testing: “We should not test Christ, as some of them did, and were killed by snakes.” Complaining: “And do not complain, as some of them did, and were killed by the destroying angel.” The summary is addressed to the letter's readers by name: “Now these things happened to them as examples and were written down as warnings for us, on whom the fulfillment of the ages has come.” Privilege is no armor: “So the one who thinks he is standing firm should be careful not to fall.”

Against the fear stands a promise measured to human strength: “No temptation has seized you except what is common to man. And God is faithful; He will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear. But when you are tempted, He will also provide an escape, so that you can stand up under it.”

So the application is flight, again: “Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry.” Then Paul argues from the table itself: “I speak to reasonable people; judge for yourselves what I say.” “Is not the cup of blessing that we bless a participation in the blood of Christ? And is not the bread that we break a participation in the body of Christ?” The table creates a body: “Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf.” Israel's altars work the same way: “Consider the people of Israel: Are not those who eat the sacrifices fellow partakers in the altar?” The idol itself is nothing; Paul has already granted that. The sacrifices behind it are not: “No, but the sacrifices of pagans are offered to demons, not to God. And I do not want you to be participants with demons.” Two tables, and no one sits at both: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons too; you cannot partake in the table of the Lord and the table of demons too.” “Are we trying to provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than He?”

The slogan returns one last time, fully answered now: “‘Everything is permissible,’ but not everything is beneficial. ‘Everything is permissible,’ but not everything is edifying.” The rule that replaces it points outward: “No one should seek his own good, but the good of others.” In practice, freedom at the market is wide: “Eat anything sold in the meat market without raising questions of conscience,” “for, ‘The earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.’” At an unbeliever's table the same freedom holds: “If an unbeliever invites you to a meal and you want to go, eat anything set before you without raising questions of conscience.” But conscience, someone else's, can close what freedom opened: “But if someone tells you, ‘This food was offered to idols,’ then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who told you and for the sake of conscience”, “the other one’s conscience, I mean, not your own.”

The whole long argument lands in one sentence of aim: “So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God.” And one of conduct: “Do not become a stumbling block, whether to Jews or Greeks or the church of God”, “as I also try to please everyone in all I do. For I am not seeking my own good, but the good of many, that they may be saved.” The section closes with its invitation, which becomes the next chapter's first line: “You are to imitate me, just as I imitate Christ.”

title: The Table of the Lord
subtitle: 1 Corinthians 11:2–34
description: The traditions carried as written, a Supper that had stopped being shared, and the words of institution against the abuse.
paragraphs: The section opens with praise, the last this part of the letter will offer: “Now I commend you for remembering me in everything and for maintaining the traditions, just as I passed them on to you.” What follows is one of the passages this letter is most argued over, and it is carried here the way the letter gives it, in Paul's own order and words, without the narration taking a side the text does not take.

The principle is stated first: “But I want you to understand that the head of every man is Christ, and the head of the woman is man, and the head of Christ is God.” From it, the practice: “Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head.” “And every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head, for it is just as if her head were shaved.” The logic is pressed: “If a woman does not cover her head, she should have her hair cut off. And if it is shameful for a woman to have her hair cut or shaved off, she should cover her head.”

Paul argues it from creation: “A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of man.” “For man did not come from woman, but woman from man.” “Neither was man created for woman, but woman for man.” “For this reason a woman ought to have a sign of authority on her head, because of the angels.” And then, in the same breath, the balance the letter itself insists on: “In the Lord, however, woman is not independent of man, nor is man independent of woman.” “For just as woman came from man, so also man is born of woman. But everything comes from God.”

He argues it from custom and from nature: “Judge for yourselves: Is it proper for a woman to pray to God with her head uncovered?” “Doesn’t nature itself teach you that if a man has long hair, it is a disgrace to him,” “but that if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? For long hair is given to her as a covering.” And he closes the dispute with the practice of all the churches: “If anyone is inclined to dispute this, we have no other practice, nor do the churches of God.”

Then the praise stops cold. “In the following instructions I have no praise to offer, because your gatherings do more harm than good.” The report this time concerns their assemblies: “First of all, I hear that when you come together as a church, there are divisions among you, and in part I believe it.” “And indeed, there must be differences among you to show which of you are approved.” At the table itself, the meal had stopped being shared: “Now then, when you come together, it is not the Lord’s Supper you eat.” “For as you eat, each of you goes ahead without sharing his meal. While one remains hungry, another gets drunk.” The question is contemptuous: “Don’t you have your own homes in which to eat and drink? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What can I say to you? Shall I praise you for this? No, I will not!”

Against the abuse, Paul sets the tradition he himself received, and its words are the ones the church has repeated ever since: “For I received from the Lord what I also passed on to you: The Lord Jesus, on the night He was betrayed, took bread,” “and when He had given thanks, He broke it and said, ‘This is My body, which is for you; do this in remembrance of Me.’” “In the same way, after supper He took the cup, saying, ‘This cup is the new covenant in My blood; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of Me.’” What the eating means: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes.”

So the table demands examination: “Therefore, whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of sinning against the body and blood of the Lord.” “Each one must examine himself before he eats of the bread and drinks of the cup.” “For anyone who eats and drinks without recognizing the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.” Paul reads their very weakness through it: “That is why many among you are weak and sick, and a number of you have fallen asleep.” And names it discipline, not doom: “Now if we judged ourselves properly, we would not come under judgment.” “But when we are judged by the Lord, we are being disciplined so that we will not be condemned with the world.”

The correction is almost embarrassingly practical: “So, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another.” “If anyone is hungry, he should eat at home, so that when you come together it will not result in judgment. And when I come, I will give instructions about the remaining matters.”

title: One Body, Many Members
subtitle: 1 Corinthians 12:1–31
description: Different gifts, the same Spirit; a body whose members cannot spare each other, arranged by God on purpose.
paragraphs: The next written question arrives with its seam showing: “Now about spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be uninformed.” Paul first reminds them where they came from: “You know that when you were pagans, you were influenced and led astray to mute idols.” Then he gives the test that sorts every spirit: “Therefore I inform you that no one who is speaking by the Spirit of God says, ‘Jesus be cursed,’ and no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except by the Holy Spirit.”

The gifts are many; their source is one, said three ways: “There are different gifts, but the same Spirit.” “There are different ministries, but the same Lord.” “There are different ways of working, but the same God works all things in all people.” And their purpose is never private: “Now to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good.” The catalogue runs through the congregation: “To one there is given through the Spirit the message of wisdom, to another the message of knowledge by the same Spirit,” “to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by that one Spirit,” “to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another distinguishing between spirits, to another speaking in various tongues, and to still another the interpretation of tongues.” Over the whole distribution stands one distributor: “All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who apportions them to each one as He determines.”

Then comes the picture the whole letter has been building toward: “The body is a unit, though it is composed of many parts. And although its parts are many, they all form one body. So it is with Christ.” The entrance into that body levels every Corinthian rank: “For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, slave or free, and we were all given one Spirit to drink.” And the body's design forbids uniformity: “For the body does not consist of one part, but of many.”

Paul lets the members argue, and their arguments refute themselves. “If the foot should say, ‘Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,’ that would not make it any less a part of the body.” “And if the ear should say, ‘Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body,’ that would not make it any less a part of the body.” A body of one organ is no body: “If the whole body were an eye, where would the sense of hearing be? If the whole body were an ear, where would the sense of smell be?” The arrangement is God's, not the members': “But in fact, God has arranged the members of the body, every one of them, according to His design.” “If they were all one part, where would the body be?” “As it is, there are many parts, but one body.”

The argument runs in the other direction too, against the honored members: “The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I do not need you.’ Nor can the head say to the feet, ‘I do not need you.’” The seemingly lesser parts carry the greater honor: “On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable,” “and the parts we consider less honorable, we treat with greater honor.” The design has a purpose: “But God has composed the body and has given greater honor to the parts that lacked it,” “so that there should be no division in the body, but that its members should have mutual concern for one another.” Its life is shared, in both directions: “If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honored, every part rejoices with it.”

Then Paul names the picture: “Now you are the body of Christ, and each of you is a member of it.” The appointments in the church follow an order: “And in the church God has appointed first of all apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then workers of miracles, and those with gifts of healing, helping, administration, and various tongues.” The closing questions expect one answer: “Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles?” “Do all have gifts of healing? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret?” No, and the no is the design. So: “But eagerly desire the greater gifts. And now I will show you the most excellent way.” The letter pauses its argument, and the most famous chapter Paul ever wrote begins.

title: The Most Excellent Way
subtitle: 1 Corinthians 13:1–13
description: Every gift weighed without love and found wanting; love described as conduct, and the three that remain.
paragraphs: The gifts argument pauses, and Paul shows the Corinthians the way that outranks every gift they were competing for. He begins at the summit of their ambitions and empties it: “If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am only a ringing gong or a clanging cymbal.” The next heights fall the same way: “If I have the gift of prophecy and can fathom all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have absolute faith so as to move mountains, but have not love, I am nothing.” And the last: “If I give all I possess to the poor and exult in the surrender of my body, but have not love, I gain nothing.” Tongues, prophecy, knowledge, faith, sacrifice: each weighed without love, and each found to be noise, nothing, or no gain.

Then love itself is described, and the description is a portrait of conduct, not feeling. “Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud.” “It is not rude, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no account of wrongs.” “Love takes no pleasure in evil, but rejoices in the truth.” Read against the letter that carries it, every line lands somewhere in Corinth: the boastful, the rude at the table, the keepers of accounts. The summary of its strength: “It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.”

Then the chapter sets love against the gifts on the scale of time: “Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will cease; where there are tongues, they will be restrained; where there is knowledge, it will be dismissed.” The gifts belong to the partial age: “For we know in part and we prophesy in part,” “but when the perfect comes, the partial passes away.”

Paul illustrates it from his own growth: “When I was a child, I talked like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I set aside childish ways.” Childish things are not condemned; they are outgrown. And the present dimness is stated as honestly as the future clarity: “Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known.”

The chapter closes by setting the three that outlast everything else in a row, and ranking them: “And now these three remain: faith, hope, and love; but the greatest of these is love.” The letter then returns to the assembly, where this love is either practiced or proved absent.

title: Order, Not Confusion
subtitle: 1 Corinthians 14:1–40
description: Intelligibility as the assembly's rule: five coherent words against ten thousand, and everything done in order.
paragraphs: The love chapter ends, and the letter returns to the gifts with its priority set: “Earnestly pursue love and eagerly desire spiritual gifts, especially the gift of prophecy.” The reason is intelligibility. A tongue speaks upward only: “For he who speaks in a tongue does not speak to men, but to God. Indeed, no one understands him; he utters mysteries in the Spirit.” Prophecy speaks across: “But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, encouragement, and comfort.” The contrast is stated as a rule of the assembly: “The one who speaks in a tongue edifies himself, but the one who prophesies edifies the church.” Paul is no enemy of the gift itself: “I wish that all of you could speak in tongues, but I would rather have you prophesy. He who prophesies is greater than one who speaks in tongues, unless he interprets so that the church may be edified.”

The test is benefit to a hearer: “Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you, unless I bring you some revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching?” Even instruments obey the rule: “Even in the case of lifeless instruments, such as the flute or harp, how will anyone recognize the tune they are playing unless the notes are distinct?” A trumpet that cannot be read cannot muster anyone: “Again, if the trumpet sounds a muffled call, who will prepare for battle?” “So it is with you. Unless you speak intelligible words with your tongue, how will anyone know what you are saying? You will just be speaking into the air.” Languages themselves are not meaningless; unknown ones are: “Assuredly, there are many different languages in the world, yet none of them is without meaning.” “If, then, I do not know the meaning of someone’s language, I am a foreigner to the speaker, and he is a foreigner to me.” So the eagerness gets its direction: “It is the same with you. Since you are eager to have spiritual gifts, strive to excel in gifts that build up the church.”

Prayer follows the same rule. The tongues-speaker should ask for the interpretation: “Therefore, the one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret.” Paul describes his own practice in both modes: “For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful.” “What then shall I do? I will pray with my spirit, but I will also pray with my mind. I will sing with my spirit, but I will also sing with my mind.” The outsider in the room decides the question: “Otherwise, if you speak a blessing in spirit, how can someone who is uninstructed say ‘Amen’ to your thanksgiving, since he does not know what you are saying?” “You may be giving thanks well enough, but the other one is not edified.” Paul's own practice is the verdict in numbers: “I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you.” “But in the church, I would rather speak five coherent words to instruct others than ten thousand words in a tongue.” And the maturity note: “Brothers, stop thinking like children. In regard to evil be infants, but in your thinking be mature.”

Scripture's word on tongues is a sobering one: “It is written in the Law:” “By strange tongues and foreign lips I will speak to this people, but even then they will not listen to Me, says the Lord.” The sign runs the opposite way from Corinth's assumption: “Tongues, then, are a sign, not for believers, but for unbelievers. Prophecy, however, is for believers, not for unbelievers.” Two visitors settle it. The tongue-filled assembly reads as madness: “So if the whole church comes together and everyone speaks in tongues, and some who are uninstructed or some unbelievers come in, will they not say that you are out of your minds?” The prophesying assembly convicts: “But if an unbeliever or uninstructed person comes in while everyone is prophesying, he will be convicted and called to account by all,” “and the secrets of his heart will be made known. So he will fall facedown and worship God, proclaiming, ‘God is truly among you!’”

Then the rules of order, concrete as house rules: “What then shall we say, brothers? When you come together, everyone has a psalm or a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. All of these must be done to build up the church.” Tongues: “If anyone speaks in a tongue, two, or at most three, should speak in turn, and someone must interpret.” “But if there is no interpreter, he should remain silent in the church and speak only to himself and God.” Prophets: “Two or three prophets should speak, and the others should weigh carefully what is said.” “And if a revelation comes to someone who is seated, the first speaker should stop.” “For you can all prophesy in turn so that everyone may be instructed and encouraged.” “The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets.” The ground of every rule: “For God is not a God of disorder, but of peace”, “as in all the churches of the saints.”

Within that same order, the letter carries the passage about women in the assembly, in its place and in its own words, and the narration here takes no side the text does not take: “Women are to be silent in the churches. They are not permitted to speak, but must be in submission, as the law says.” “If they wish to inquire about something, they are to ask their own husbands at home; for it is dishonorable for a woman to speak in the church.” Paul will not let Corinth treat its practice as the standard: “Did the word of God originate with you? Or are you the only ones it has reached?” And he claims the Lord's authority for the whole instruction: “If anyone considers himself a prophet or spiritual person, let him acknowledge that what I am writing you is the Lord’s command.” “But if anyone ignores this, he himself will be ignored.”

The chapter, and the whole gifts section, closes by balancing both commands at once: “So, my brothers, be eager to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues.” “But everything must be done in a proper and orderly manner.”

title: He Appeared to Cephas
subtitle: 1 Corinthians 15:1–34
description: The gospel received and handed on, named witnesses, and the chain that follows if Christ has not been raised.
paragraphs: The letter's last great argument begins with a reminder, not a new teaching: “Now, brothers, I want to remind you of the gospel I preached to you, which you received, and in which you stand firm.” The gospel is the ground of their salvation, on one condition: “By this gospel you are saved, if you hold firmly to the word I preached to you. Otherwise, you have believed in vain.”

Then Paul hands over what he himself had been handed, and the creed is quoted here whole, in the letter's own order, exactly as he says he received it: “For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures,” “that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,” “and that He appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve.” “After that, He appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once, most of whom are still living, though some have fallen asleep.” “Then He appeared to James, then to all the apostles.” “And last of all He appeared to me also, as to one of untimely birth.” The list stands as the letter gives it, witnesses named and numbered, most of them alive when Paul wrote and able to be asked.

The last witness examines himself: “For I am the least of the apostles and am unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.” What made him an apostle at all was not merit: “But by the grace of God I am what I am, and His grace to me was not in vain. No, I worked harder than all of them”, “yet not I, but the grace of God that was with me.” Whoever preached it, the message is one: “Whether, then, it was I or they, this is what we preach, and this is what you believed.”

Against that foundation, Paul sets the Corinthian denial and follows it without flinching: “But if it is preached that Christ has been raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?” The chain runs link by link: “If there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised.” “And if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is worthless, and so is your faith.” Worse follows: “In that case, we are also exposed as false witnesses about God. For we have testified about God that He raised Christ from the dead, but He did not raise Him if in fact the dead are not raised.” The chain circles back tighter: “For if the dead are not raised, then not even Christ has been raised.” “And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins.” The dead in Christ are gone for good: “Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished.” And the apostles become the most pitiable of men: “If our hope in Christ is for this life alone, we are to be pitied more than all men.”

Then the reversal, stated as fact: “But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.” Firstfruits means a harvest follows, and the two men frame it: “For since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead comes also through a man.” “For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive.” The order is given, and it is carried here as the letter writes it, without diagram or addition: “But each in his own turn: Christ the firstfruits; then at His coming, those who belong to Him.” “Then the end will come, when He hands over the kingdom to God the Father after He has destroyed all dominion, authority, and power.” “For He must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet.” “The last enemy to be destroyed is death.” Scripture's own line stands inside the argument: “God has put everything under His feet.” And the letter qualifies it in its own words: “Now when it says that everything has been put under Him, this clearly does not include the One who put everything under Him.” “And when all things have been subjected to Him, then the Son Himself will be made subject to Him who put all things under Him, so that God may be all in all.”

Paul then points at a practice and lets it argue. The verse stands as the single verse it is, in its place, unexpanded: “If these things are not so, what will those do who are baptized for the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized for them?” And at his own danger: “And why do we endanger ourselves every hour?” “I face death every day, brothers, as surely as I boast about you in Christ Jesus our Lord.” The Ephesus arena is named with its condition attached: “If I fought wild beasts in Ephesus for human motives, what did I gain? If the dead are not raised,” then the world's own motto follows: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”

The warning proverb stands in the letter's own quotation marks: “Do not be deceived:” “Bad company corrupts good character.” And the section ends with a sobering command, aimed at ignorance Paul calls shameful: “Sober up as you ought, and stop sinning; for some of you are ignorant of God. I say this to your shame.” One question remains, and it is about the body itself. The letter takes it up next.

title: Death Swallowed Up
subtitle: 1 Corinthians 15:35–58
description: A seed and its body, splendor fitted to everything, the trumpet, the taunt over death, and work that is not in vain.
paragraphs: The objection arrives in an opponent's voice, and Paul quotes it fairly: “But someone will ask, ‘How are the dead raised? With what kind of body will they come?’” His answer begins with a rebuke and a farm: “You fool! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies.” The seed is not the plant it becomes: “And what you sow is not the body that will be, but just a seed, perhaps of wheat or something else.” The body it gets is God's assignment: “But God gives it a body as He has designed, and to each kind of seed He gives its own body.”

Variety is built into creation at every level: “Not all flesh is the same: Men have one kind of flesh, animals have another, birds another, and fish another.” “There are also heavenly bodies and earthly bodies. But the splendor of the heavenly bodies is of one degree, and the splendor of the earthly bodies is of another.” “The sun has one degree of splendor, the moon another, and the stars another; and star differs from star in splendor.” God, who fits every seed and every star with its own body and glory, is not stuck for a body for the dead.

Then the application, in the chapter's great drumbeat of pairs: “So will it be with the resurrection of the dead: What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable.” “It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power.” “It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body.” Scripture's Adam stands behind the contrast: “So it is written:” “The first man Adam became a living being”; “the last Adam a life-giving spirit.” The order runs one way: “The spiritual, however, was not first, but the natural, and then the spiritual.” “The first man was of the dust of the earth, the second man from heaven.” “As was the earthly man, so also are those who are of the earth; and as is the heavenly man, so also are those who are of heaven.” And the destiny of the second family: “And just as we have borne the likeness of the earthly man, so also shall we bear the likeness of the heavenly man.”

What the present body cannot do is stated without flinching: “Now I declare to you, brothers, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable.” So a change is necessary, and Paul announces it as a disclosed secret: “Listen, I tell you a mystery: We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed”, “in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, the dead will be raised imperishable, and we will be changed.” The clothing image carries the necessity: “For the perishable must be clothed with the imperishable, and the mortal with immortality.”

Then Scripture's taunt is placed on the church's lips in advance: “When the perishable has been clothed with the imperishable and the mortal with immortality, then the saying that is written will come to pass:” “Death has been swallowed up in victory.” “Where, O Death, is your victory? Where, O Death, is your sting?” The sting is diagnosed, not denied: “The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.” And the chapter's thanksgiving breaks through: “But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ!”

After the trumpet, the letter ends the argument where it always ends, with work on the ground: “Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast and immovable. Always excel in the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain.” The resurrection chapter, the most cosmic in the letter, closes by telling ordinary believers that nothing they do for the Lord is wasted.

title: My Love Be With All of You
subtitle: 1 Corinthians 16:1–24
description: The collection, the road through Macedonia, Apollos in God's time, and a greeting in Paul's own hand.
paragraphs: The last chapter opens with the final written question, marked by its seam: “Now about the collection for the saints, you are to do as I directed the churches of Galatia:”. The practice is regular and quiet: “On the first day of every week, each of you should set aside a portion of his income, saving it up, so that when I come no collections will be needed.” The gift travels with the church's own chosen carriers: “Then, on my arrival, I will send letters with those you recommend to carry your gift to Jerusalem.” “And if it is advisable for me to go also, they can travel with me.”

Then Paul lays out his road, and the letter finally names the city it was written from. Macedonia first: “After I go through Macedonia, however, I will come to you; for I will be going through Macedonia.” Corinth gets more than a stopover: “Perhaps I will stay with you awhile, or even spend the winter, so that you can help me on my journey, wherever I go.” “For I do not want to see you now only in passing; I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits.” For now he stays put, and says why: “But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost,” “because a great door for effective work has opened to me, even though many oppose me.” An open door and opposition, together, in one sentence.

Two men are commended to Corinth's care. Timothy first: “If Timothy comes, see to it that he has nothing to fear while he is with you, for he is doing the work of the Lord, just as I am.” “No one, then, should treat him with contempt. Send him on his way in peace so that he can return to me, for I am expecting him along with the brothers.” Then Apollos, and the note is careful, given what Corinth had made of his name: “Now about our brother Apollos: I strongly urged him to go to you with the brothers. He was not at all inclined to go now, but he will go when he has the opportunity.” The man whose name had been a faction's banner would not be sent on a faction's errand. He would come in God's time, not Paul's scheduling.

Four short commands stand like a watchword before the greetings: “Be on the alert. Stand firm in the faith. Be men of courage. Be strong.” “Do everything in love.” Then the letter honors the household that had carried Corinth's questions to Ephesus: “You know that Stephanas and his household were the first converts in Achaia, and they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints. Now I urge you, brothers,” “to submit to such as these, and to every fellow worker and laborer.” The delegation itself is named with thanks: “I am glad that Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus have arrived, because they have supplied what was lacking from you.” “For they refreshed my spirit and yours as well. Show your appreciation, therefore, to such men.”

The greetings circle wide: “The churches in the province of Asia send you greetings. Aquila and Prisca greet you warmly in the Lord, and so does the church that meets at their house.” The tentmakers of Acts 18, Corinth's own former hosts, now in Ephesus with a church under their roof. “All the brothers here send you greetings. Greet one another with a holy kiss.”

Then the letter's authentication, displayed the way the Thessalonian letter displayed it: Paul takes the pen himself. “This greeting is in my own hand”, and the name after the dash is simply Paul. In his own hand he writes the sharpest line in the closing, and it is carried here as he wrote it: “If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be under a curse. Come, O Lord!” And then the last two sentences of the letter, grace and love together: “The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you.” “My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen.”
